status: in progress — chapters 1-36 (the primeval history, Abraham, and Jacob) indexed; 37-50 pending
note: Indexed in sections along the book's own seams: the primeval history (1-11), Abraham (12-25:18), Jacob (25:19-36), and Joseph (37-50). The indexing order named chapter 18 the classic PR20 text and expected C14 and C01; chapter 18 falls in the second section.
sectioning_note: As with Jeremiah and Deuteronomy, the status field names what is done.
coverage_note: Chapters 1-11, unindexed: the sons of God and the Nephilim (6:1-4), which the index does not interpret; the genealogies of chapter 5 (except Enoch, 5:21-24), chapter 10, and 11:10-32; and the curse on Canaan (9:24-27). The last is left out deliberately. It was used for centuries to justify the enslavement of Africans, on a reading the text does not support — Canaan, not Ham, is cursed, and the Canaanites are not African — and the index will not place a formation tag on a passage with that history without saying so. The entry at 9:20-23 stops before it. Also left out: the birth of Seth and the first calling on the name (4:25-26), and the end of Noah's life (9:28-29). Chapters 12-25: the war of the kings (14:1-12, folded into the rescue entry as its setting), the boundary list of 15:18-21 (folded into its pericope), the assault at Lot's door with Lot's offer of his daughters (19:1-11), and the incest of Lot's daughters (19:30-38). Lot's hospitality in 19:1-3 is real, and the index declines to tag hospitality on a passage in which the host offers his daughters to a mob. Also left out: Nahor's descendants (22:20-24) and the genealogies of Keturah's and Ishmael's sons (25:12-18). Chapters 25:19-36: Esau's wives (26:34-35, 27:46-28:9), Jacob's breeding of the flocks (30:25-43), the flight from Laban and Rachel's theft of the teraphim (31:1-35, the setting of the entry at 31:36-55), the arrival at Shechem (33:18-20), and Esau's genealogy (36).

entries.pericope: God saw everything that he had made, and, behold, it was very good
entries.connection: The world is ordered by a word, divided and named, and pronounced good seven times — 'very good' at the end. C01's claim that reality has a grain begins here: the order is not imposed on a neutral world but is the world. The scale and the refrain are the landscape C24 asks the reader to stand before in wonder. And the unit of the whole account is the day — 'there was evening and there was morning' — ending in a day of rest made holy, which is C28's unit of formation from the first page of scripture.

entries.pericope: To dress it and to keep it
entries.connection: The man is formed from dust and given breath, and his first assignment is work: put into the garden 'to dress it and to keep it.' Work belongs to the world before anything went wrong, which is the ground of C13's ordinary faithfulness — the daily task is not a punishment to be escaped into spirituality. The single prohibition sets the moral order of C01 in its simplest form: freedom everywhere, and one limit.

entries.pericope: It is not good that the man should be alone
entries.connection: The first thing in creation pronounced not good is solitude. The answer is a companion who is 'bone of my bones,' and the passage closes on a household — leaving father and mother, one flesh, naked and not ashamed. C14 begins from the same conviction: the household is not a distraction from formation but one of its primary places.

entries.pericope: Has God really said?
entries.connection: The failure arrives as a question, and the damage is done in the conversation that follows. She engages the thought, amends the command in reply, listens to the counter-claim — and then the sequence: she saw that it was good for food, a delight to the eyes, desired to make one wise; she took, ate, gave. Watchfulness holds that destructive thoughts do their damage 'during the hospitality, not the arrival,' and this is the hospitality narrated step by step. The progression from perception through desire to act is the anatomy of a failure that C21 teaches Cassian's way, given here in a single verse (3:6).

entries.pericope: The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me of the tree
entries.connection: Asked a direct question, the man blames the woman and, in the same breath, the God who gave her; the woman blames the serpent. Neither looks at their own portion. Self-Accusation asks, in any friction, what is my portion here, before assigning anyone else's — and asks 'how fast is my blaming reflex?' This is the reflex at its origin, two sentences after the first sin. C22 teaches the practice; the question that precedes the blaming — 'Where are you?' — is God seeking rather than prosecuting, which is C19's shepherd.

entries.pericope: Yahweh God made coats of skins for Adam and for his wife, and clothed them
entries.connection: The consequences are pronounced in full — pain, toil, thorns, dust — and the moral order of C01 does not bend. Then, before the expulsion, a single act of care: God makes them clothing and dresses them himself. The fig leaves were their own covering for their shame; the coats are his. C19's door is open even on the day the garden closes.

entries.pericope: Sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it
entries.connection: God speaks to Cain at the exact moment Watchfulness is for: the anger has arrived and the face has fallen, but nothing has been done. 'Why are you angry?… sin crouches at the door. Its desire is for you, but you are to rule over it.' The image is of something waiting at the gate, not yet inside, and the instruction is to master it there. Cain does not, and the next verse is a murder. The practice and its absence in two sentences, with the interior cause — anger at a brother's acceptance — traced by God before it is acted on, which is C21's diagnosis.

entries.pericope: Am I my brother's keeper?
entries.connection: 'I don't know. Am I my brother's keeper?' — a lie and a denial of responsibility in one answer, the opposite of the honest naming C04's audit asks for. The judgment is real: the blood cries from the ground, and Cain is driven out. And yet when Cain says the punishment is more than he can bear, God marks him so that no one will kill him. Mercy set as a limit around the guilty, which is C19's door kept ajar even for a murderer.

entries.pericope: If Cain will be avenged seven times, truly Lamech seventy-seven times
entries.connection: Lamech's song boasts of killing a young man for a wound and multiplies vengeance past what God had set: seven times for Cain, seventy-seven for Lamech. Retaliation escalating as a matter of pride. Non-Retaliation is the refusal to return evil for evil, and this is its absence celebrated in verse. The number returns in Matthew 18:22, where forgiveness is commanded to seventy times seven — the same arithmetic turned the other way, which is the move C03 and C27 both make.

entries.pericope: Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him
entries.connection: In a genealogy where every other entry ends 'then he died,' one man 'walked with God' — said twice — 'and he was not, for God took him.' Nothing else is recorded of him. A life described entirely by companionship with God is C11's remaining, and a life whose only record is that companionship is C23's hidden life.

entries.pericope: It grieved him in his heart
entries.connection: The diagnosis reaches the root: 'every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually' — not the acts but the imagination producing them, which is where C21 looks. And God's response to it is grief before it is judgment: 'Yahweh was sorry that he had made man… and it grieved him in his heart.' C27's measure of the mature heart is that it cannot delight in another's condemnation; the first thing said of God's heart in scripture is that it grieved.

entries.pericope: Thus Noah did. According to all that God commanded him, so he did
entries.connection: Noah is righteous, blameless in his generation, and 'walked with God,' and what that looks like is construction: a ship to exact dimensions, provisions gathered, animals brought in. 'Thus Noah did. According to all that God commanded him, so he did' — said twice. Faithfulness as a long, practical, unspectacular job carried out to specification in a hostile world, which is C13's.

entries.pericope: He stayed yet another seven days
entries.connection: 'God remembered Noah' — the turn of the story is God's memory. Then a long waiting, told in detail: the raven, the dove that finds no rest, seven days, the dove with the olive leaf, seven days more, the dove that does not return. Noah does not leave the ship until he is told. C25's patience with a process that cannot be hurried and can only be checked, step by step. PR14 shares the patience but is defined as the patience of growth, and the waiting here is for the waters, so it is not tagged.

entries.pericope: I will not again curse the ground any more for man's sake, because the imagination of man's heart is evil
entries.connection: The reason given for never repeating the flood is the same as the reason given for sending it: the imagination of man's heart is evil from youth. Mercy grounded in realism rather than in improvement, which is C19's door. The covenant that follows is made 'with every living creature' — the widest circle in the Old Testament, C27's — and the life of every human is protected 'for God made man in his own image,' the ground of C01's moral order. Seedtime and harvest, day and night, 'shall not cease.'

entries.pericope: They went in backwards, and covered the nakedness of their father
entries.connection: Noah is drunk and uncovered in his tent. Ham sees, and goes out and tells his brothers. Shem and Japheth take a garment on their shoulders, walk in backwards, cover their father, and keep their faces turned away so that they do not see. Covering Weakness is the refusal to expose someone whose failure would shame them, absorbing the inconvenience oneself to protect their dignity. Here it is enacted with its counter-example in the same scene: one son exposes, two cover, and the covering is done so as not even to look. The strongest narrative anchor for PR17 in the index. God's own clothing of Adam and Eve (3:21) is the precedent. The curse on Canaan that follows (9:24-27) is not indexed; see the coverage note.

entries.pericope: Let's make ourselves a name
entries.connection: The builders' motive is stated in their own words: 'let's build ourselves a city, and a tower whose top reaches to the sky, and let's make ourselves a name, lest we be scattered.' Achievement aimed at reputation, and security sought in a monument. The Hidden Life is the practice against exactly this — the reach for the audience, the energy spent on being perceived — and the tower is its absence at the scale of a civilisation, with its cost: the work is stopped and the builders scattered. C18's detachment is the other half: the tower is built to hold on. Confidence is medium; the passage is about collective ambition, and the practice is personal.

entries.pericope: Get out of your country… to the land that I will show you
entries.connection: The call gives a direction and withholds the destination — 'to the land that I will show you' — and the response is one sentence: 'So Abram went.' He arrives in a land where 'the Canaanite was then in the land,' builds altars, and keeps moving. C17's citizen-stranger begins as a man living in tents in someone else's country, and C18's detachment as leaving a father's house on a word. Hebrews 11 will read the whole life this way.

entries.pericope: Please say that you are my sister
entries.connection: Fear produces a lie that endangers his wife and enriches himself, and it is the foreign king who rebukes the man of promise: 'What is this that you have done to me?' The narrator records it without softening. C21 traces failure to its root, and here the root is named in Abram's own words — 'they will kill me' — while C04's mirror is held up by an outsider.

entries.pericope: Let there be no strife between me and you… for we are relatives
entries.connection: Strife between the herdsmen, and the elder man, who has the right to choose, gives the choice away: 'Isn't the whole land before you?… If you go to the left hand, then I will go to the right.' The objective is changed from winning to keeping the relationship, and the concession is made first and out loud — the Architecture of Peace in its plainest narrative form. Lot chooses by what his eyes see, the well-watered plain 'like the garden of Yahweh,' which is toward Sodom: C07's lesson that what we see depends on what we want.

entries.pericope: When Abram heard that his relative was taken captive
entries.connection: Lot separated from Abram, took the better land, and moved toward Sodom. When Lot is carried off in a war that is no concern of Abram's, Abram arms his household and goes after him as far as Damascus. Unobligated Loyalty is fidelity in a season of difficulty when one is free to walk away; nothing obliged Abram to a nephew who had chosen against him, and he went. Confidence is medium because kinship carried real obligation in the ancient world, and the text gives no motive beyond 'his relative.'

entries.pericope: I will not take a thread nor a sandal strap
entries.connection: Offered the spoil by the king of Sodom, Abram refuses all of it — 'not a thread nor a sandal strap… lest you should say, I have made Abram rich' — while insisting that his allies receive their share. Detachment that protects his independence from a corrupt patron, C18's, and authority that guards the portion of those who fought with him, C16's. The tithe to Melchizedek and his blessing frame the refusal.

entries.pericope: What will you give me, since I go childless?
entries.connection: The promise of reward is answered with the grief underneath it: 'Lord Yahweh, what will you give me, since I go childless?' — said twice, plainly, to God's face. God does not rebuke the complaint; he takes Abram outside and tells him to count the stars 'if you are able.' Sacred Lament is the honest expression of grief before God without abandoning hope and without demanding immediate resolution, and Abram's next act is to believe. The night sky as the measure of the promise is C24's. Confidence is medium; the complaint is brief, and the book's stronger lament material lies in Psalms and Job.

entries.pericope: The iniquity of the Amorite is not yet full
entries.connection: A covenant cut in the dark, and a timetable longer than a life: four hundred years of affliction for his descendants, his own death 'in a good old age' before any of it is fulfilled, and judgment on the land's inhabitants deferred because their iniquity 'is not yet full.' C25's long view, in which God's purposes are measured in generations and no one sees the end of what he began.

entries.pericope: You are a God who sees
entries.connection: Sarai gives her servant to Abram, then blames him for the result — 'This wrong is your fault' — and Abram hands Hagar back to Sarai's power: 'Do to her whatever is good in your eyes.' The blaming reflex and the abdication of responsibility, both counter-examples, Sarai's of Self-Accusation (medium: she has a real grievance against Hagar's contempt, and the practice does not require silence about it). Then the one with least power is the one God finds, in the wilderness, and she names him: 'You are a God who sees.' C16's why-the-vulnerable-specifically and C19's shepherd seeking. The angel's instruction to return (16:9) is not read here as counsel to return to harsh treatment; the index does not commend it, and the curriculum's guard against loyalty that keeps someone in harm applies.

entries.pericope: Walk before me, and be blameless
entries.connection: At ninety-nine, a command and a covenant: 'Walk before me, and be blameless.' Names changed, a sign given, and Abraham's response mixes laughter at the impossibility with a father's plea for the son who will not be the heir — 'Oh that Ishmael might live before you!' — which God hears. The circumcision of the whole household 'in the same day' is obedience without delay. C25's walk, given at the end of a long life rather than the beginning, and C14's household carried into the covenant together.

entries.pericope: He ran to meet them from the tent door
entries.connection: The indexing order called this the classic text for the Sacrifice of Routine. Abraham is sitting at the tent door 'in the heat of the day,' the hour of rest, when three strangers appear. He runs to them, bows, begs them not to pass by, and then everything in the household moves: Sarah to the flour, Abraham running to the herd, the best calf, butter and milk. He offers 'a morsel of bread' and serves a feast, and he stands by them under the tree while they eat. PR20 is letting hospitality override one's own routine when a guest arrives, making the visitor comfortable without display. All of that is here. Confidence is medium for one reason: what is overridden is the midday rest, not a religious discipline, which is the specific thing the Desert Fathers' practice has in view.

entries.pericope: No, but you did laugh
entries.connection: Sarah laughs at the promise, denies it out of fear, and is answered with the plain fact and nothing more: 'No, but you did laugh.' The denial is named without being punished. 'Is anything too hard for Yahweh?' is C24's question, and the gentle refusal to accept the lie is C04's honesty without condemnation.

entries.pericope: Shouldn't the Judge of all the earth do right?
entries.connection: Told that Sodom is to be judged, Abraham stands before God and argues for the city — fifty, forty-five, forty, thirty, twenty, ten — calling himself 'dust and ashes' and pressing anyway. He is pleading for the spared place, not only for his nephew. Shedding Harshness widens the circle of concern until no one stands outside it, and its practice is to pray for the good of those one has every reason to write off; this is that prayer, made for the most notorious city in scripture. The reason God discloses his plan is C14's: Abraham is to 'command his children and his household after him… to do righteousness and justice.'

entries.pericope: But he lingered; and the men grabbed his hand… Yahweh being merciful to him
entries.connection: Warned, Lot cannot persuade his sons-in-law, who think he is joking, and at dawn he lingers — so the angels take him by the hand and put him outside, 'Yahweh being merciful to him.' Mercy that drags the reluctant out, which is C19's. His wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt: the cost of being unable to let go of what is being left, C18's warning in its starkest image. The narrator ends with Abraham at dawn looking at the smoke, and 'God remembered Abraham, and sent Lot out.' The assault at Lot's door and Lot's offer of his daughters (19:1-11) are not indexed; see the coverage note.

entries.pericope: Surely the fear of God is not in this place
entries.connection: The same lie as in Egypt, and the same reversal: the foreign king is the one with 'integrity of heart,' and Abraham's excuse exposes his assumption — 'I thought, Surely the fear of God is not in this place.' A prejudice about outsiders, proved false by the outsider. C21's diagnosis of fear as the root, and C04's mirror, again held up by someone the man of promise had written off. Abraham's prayer for Abimelech's household, at the end, is the repair.

entries.pericope: God has made me laugh. Everyone who hears will laugh with me
entries.connection: The laughter of disbelief in chapter 18 becomes the laughter of joy, and the child is named for it. 'At the set time of which God had spoken' — a promise kept on its own schedule, twenty-five years after it was given. C10's joy as something received, and C25's long wait with a definite end.

entries.pericope: God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water
entries.connection: Hagar and her son are sent into the wilderness with bread and a skin of water. When the water is gone she puts the boy under a bush and sits a bowshot away — 'Don't let me see the death of the child' — and lifts up her voice and weeps. 'God heard the voice of the boy.' Grief voiced without restraint in the far place, and heard: Sacred Lament at medium, since her weeping is not addressed to God by name, though the text answers it as though it were. Then 'God opened her eyes, and she saw a well' — the water was already there. C06 is built around exactly that kind of seeing, given rather than achieved. C19's door opens for the one cast out.

entries.pericope: Abraham complained to Abimelech because of a water well
entries.connection: A grievance raised honestly — the well seized by Abimelech's servants — and answered: 'I don't know who has done this thing.' Abraham does not press for a verdict; he gives sheep and cattle and sets aside seven lambs as a witness, and the two make a covenant. The dispute is resolved by repair rather than victory, which is the Architecture of Peace. Medium, because the gift also secures his claim to the well.

entries.pericope: God will provide himself the lamb
entries.connection: 'Take your son, your only son, whom you love.' Abraham rises early, saddles the donkey, splits the wood, and walks three days. To his son's question he answers, 'God will provide himself the lamb, my son,' and the text says twice, 'they both went together.' The index tags what the passage plainly shows: a man not withholding what he loves most, C18's detachment at its most extreme, and a trust that walks forward without understanding, C24's. PR04 was considered for the latter and not tagged; the passage is a test of obedience, and reading it as a discipline of unknowing would be to explain it, which the narrator conspicuously declines to do.

entries.pericope: I am a stranger and a foreigner living with you
entries.connection: Sarah dies, and Abraham mourns and weeps. Then he negotiates for a grave as what he is — 'a stranger and a foreigner living with you' — bowing to the people of the land, declining a gift, and paying the full price in public 'according to the current merchants' standard.' Full, courteous, honest participation in the life of a society that is not his, while the burial itself is an act of faith in a promise about the land. The Citizen-Stranger's posture, conducted at a graveside.

entries.pericope: I will also draw for your camels, until they have done drinking
entries.connection: The servant prays for a sign of kindness and receives more than he asked: a stranger at a well gives him water and then, unasked, draws for all ten camels, running back and forth 'until they have done drinking.' Spontaneous Service is pausing one's own work to help someone finish theirs, and treating the interruption as the work; she was there to fill her own pitcher. The servant's faithfulness to an absent master — praying, watching in silence, worshipping when the answer comes — is C13's ordinary faithfulness and C16's stewardship.

entries.pericope: I will not eat until I have told my message
entries.connection: Food is set before a traveller who has come four hundred miles, and he refuses it until he has delivered his errand. The story is retold in full so that the household can judge it for themselves, and Rebekah herself is asked: 'Will you go with this man?' 'I will go.' C13's faithfulness of a servant who puts the task before his own comfort, and C14's household that consults the one whose life is being decided.

entries.pericope: Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the evening
entries.connection: Isaac is introduced alone, in a field, at evening, meditating — and looks up to see the camels. The marriage ends the chapter with three short clauses: she became his wife, he loved her, and 'Isaac was comforted after his mother's death.' C09's solitary place of prayer, and C14's household as the place where grief is comforted.

entries.pericope: Isaac and Ishmael, his sons, buried him
entries.connection: Abraham dies 'in a good old age, an old man, and full of years,' and the two sons whose mothers were set against each other, one of whom was sent into the wilderness, bury him together in the field he bought. The narrator makes nothing of it. C15's peace, recorded at a grave rather than negotiated, and C25's life completed at the pace it was given.

entries.pericope: Isaac loved Esau, because he ate his venison. Rebekah loved Jacob
entries.connection: Twins struggling in the womb, and a mother who brings the struggle to God — 'If it be so, why do I live?' Then the sentence that sets up the whole cycle: each parent loves one son, and the father's love is given a reason as small as a taste for game. C14's household, with the partiality named in the place it will do most damage.

entries.pericope: Behold, I am about to die. What good is the birthright to me?
entries.connection: A famished man trades his inheritance for a bowl of stew, persuaded by the hunger of the moment that nothing else matters — 'I am about to die' — and 'so Esau despised his birthright.' C02's first truth is seeing the end of the path; here the end is traded for the next five minutes. The impulse allowed to decide is C20's territory. The brother who exploits the hunger is no example either, and the narrator lets both stand.

entries.pericope: She is my sister… lest I die because of her
entries.connection: Isaac tells his father's lie, in the same place, for the same reason, a generation later. Interior Diagnosis asks what behaviour keeps returning in a new form, and what is underneath all its versions; this is the pattern no one in the family has traced, answered at the level of a household — the fear and the evasion pass from father to son unexamined, and the foreign king has to name it. C21's root, and C14's household as the place it is handed down.

entries.pericope: For now Yahweh has made room for us
entries.connection: Envied and expelled, Isaac re-digs his father's wells. The herdsmen of Gerar claim the first — 'Contention' — and he moves on; they claim the second — 'Enmity' — and he moves on; the third no one disputes, and he names it 'Room.' Nothing returned for what was taken twice. Then the king who sent him away arrives seeking a treaty, and Isaac names the injury plainly — 'Why have you come to me, since you hate me?' — and makes them a feast. Non-Retaliation in the yielding, and the Architecture of Peace in the table set for those who had wronged him: the grievance spoken, and the aim repair.

entries.pericope: Bless me, even me also, my father
entries.connection: A blind father, a mother's plan, a son's deception repeated to his father's face — 'I am Esau your firstborn' — and the other son's 'exceeding great and bitter cry.' Every member of the household is complicit or wronged, and the partiality of 25:28 bears its fruit. C14's household at its most divided; C04's mirror is the narrator's refusal to excuse anyone.

entries.pericope: Your brother Esau comforts himself about you by planning to kill you
entries.connection: 'Esau said in his heart' — the thought is quoted as it is entertained — and Rebekah names what it is doing for him: he 'comforts himself… by planning to kill you.' A grievance nursed into a plan because the nursing feels like relief. Watchfulness says destructive thoughts do their damage during the hospitality, not the arrival; here the hospitality has become the comfort. C22's measure of the healed heart is what anger is allowed to do once it has arrived.

entries.pericope: Surely Yahweh is in this place, and I didn't know it
entries.connection: A fugitive sleeping on a stone at sunset sees a stairway with angels on it and wakes saying, 'Surely Yahweh is in this place, and I didn't know it.' Presence was already there; sight was what was missing. C06's opening of the eyes, and C09's secret place found in the least likely spot — 'this is none other than God's house, and this is the gate of heaven.' His vow is conditional, and the index does not tidy it.

entries.pericope: They seemed to him but a few days, for the love he had for her
entries.connection: Seven years of labour 'seemed to him but a few days, for the love he had for her.' C10's movement from duty to delight in one sentence: the same work, transformed by what it is for. Then the deceiver is deceived, in the dark, and the excuse given turns on birth order — 'it is not done so in our place, to give the younger before the firstborn.' C01's grain: the younger son who took the elder's blessing is given the elder daughter.

entries.pericope: This time will I praise Yahweh
entries.connection: 'Yahweh saw that Leah was hated.' She names her sons out of her grief and says it to God each time: 'Yahweh has looked at my affliction. For now my husband will love me'; 'Yahweh has heard that I am hated'; 'now this time will my husband be joined to me.' Then the fourth: 'This time will I praise Yahweh.' Sacred Lament brought honestly before God, and its test — sorrow that moves through and leaves one softer rather than curdling — passed in four names. The release from needing her husband's love before she can praise is C18's freedom, and the God who sees the unloved is C19's.

entries.pericope: Rachel envied her sister
entries.connection: 'Give me children, or else I will die' — and Jacob's anger: 'Am I in God's place?' Two sisters bargain over servants, sons, and mandrakes, and Rachel names a son 'with mighty wrestlings have I wrestled with my sister, and have prevailed.' C22 locates conflict in its source, and the source is named in the first verse: envy. 'God remembered Rachel' at the end is the narrator's mercy, not a resolution of the rivalry.

entries.pericope: In the day the drought consumed me, and the frost by night
entries.connection: After twenty years, Jacob finally states his case: the losses he bore himself, the heat and frost, the sleep that fled, wages changed ten times. Faithful work under a master who cheated him, which is C13's ordinary faithfulness tested under injustice. The covenant that ends it is a boundary rather than a reconciliation — 'Yahweh watch between me and you, when we are absent one from another' — peace as an agreed line neither will cross 'for harm,' which is the minimal form of C15. PR23 shares the honest work, but it is narrated here as a grievance rather than enacted, and is not tagged.

entries.pericope: I am not worthy of the least of all the loving kindnesses
entries.connection: Told that Esau is coming with four hundred men, Jacob divides his camp in fear and then prays: 'I am not worthy of the least of all the loving kindnesses, and of all the truth, which you have shown to your servant; for with just my staff I passed over this Jordan.' The first prayer of his life that is not a bargain. C09's place of prayer reached under threat, and C19's grace acknowledged as unearned. The waves of gifts sent ahead are still a strategy, and the narrator records both.

entries.pericope: I won't let you go, unless you bless me
entries.connection: Alone at the ford, he wrestles until daybreak with someone he cannot overcome and will not release, and he comes away with a new name and a limp. Transformation as a change of name — of nature — received in a struggle and marked permanently in the body: C26's change, which does not leave a person as they were. The opponent will not give his name — 'Why is it that you ask what my name is?' — and Jacob names the place for what he saw and survived, which is C24's posture before what cannot be grasped.

entries.pericope: Esau ran to meet him, embraced him, fell on his neck, kissed him, and they wept
entries.connection: Jacob approaches bowing seven times, the brother he cheated in front of four hundred men. Esau runs, embraces him, falls on his neck, kisses him, and they weep; Luke 15:20 uses nearly the same words for the father of the prodigal. 'I have enough, my brother.' Merciful Reintegration is receiving the one who wronged you back without lingering shame or probation, and Esau's welcome sets no terms at all. Jacob's reply — 'I have seen your face, as one sees the face of God' — joins the reconciliation to the night before. Confidence is high on the act and the tag; the text never has Jacob say he is sorry, and the practice's 'once repentance is clear' is read here from his posture.

entries.pericope: Should he deal with our sister as with a prostitute?
entries.connection: Dinah is taken and violated; she never speaks in the chapter. Her father 'held his peace.' Her brothers answer with deceit and then, while the men of the city are recovering from the circumcision they demanded, kill every male and plunder the rest. Jacob's only rebuke concerns his own danger. Non-Retaliation's absence at its most catastrophic: a real wrong, answered with a slaughter that multiplies it and destroys the innocent with the guilty. The index does not treat the wrong to Dinah as small; it is the reason the vengeance has a claim on the reader's sympathy, and the reason the passage is the clearest counter-example in Genesis. C21's anger traced to its root, and C16's failure of the head of the house to act for the one who was harmed.

entries.pericope: Put away the foreign gods that are among you
entries.connection: Called back to the place of his vow, Jacob has his household give up the foreign gods and earrings, bury them under an oak, wash, and change their clothes before they go up. A return to the beginning after twenty years of drift, prepared for by putting things away — C19's return, and C20's clearing of what had been allowed in. The name Israel is confirmed at Bethel.

entries.pericope: She named him Benoni, but his father named him Benjamin
entries.connection: Rachel dies in childbirth on the road and names her son Son of My Sorrow; his father renames him Son of the Right Hand. A child not left to carry the name of the grief he was born into. The chapter ends with Isaac's death, 'old and full of days,' and two sons who once planned murder burying their father together. C14's household carried through its losses, and C15's peace, held.
